headline: High: Cursor’s broad filesystem/network access can leak or corrupt RD-Agent’s shared workspace, while RD-Agent’s API-driven research outputs can be misused by Cursor without verification.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor reads and writes workspace files, open buffers, and clipboard contents, and shares state via the local filesystem; RD-Agent also uses files/logs and can ingest outputs from its research/development agents. That creates a plausible instruction-hijack path through shared files or copied content, though not a direct documented bridge.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or log directory, injected instructions in files can cross from one agent to the other.
IF Cursor auto-runs tool output from a file or clipboard, attacker-controlled text can steer its agent loop.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable clipboard-based handoff between agents.
Review any file before the other agent reads it.
Turn off Cursor Yolo mode for shared projects.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to shared files.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor touches source code, open files, and clipboard contents and has broad network egress; RD-Agent handles research data, execution traces, logs, and API keys. If they share a workspace, either agent can expose the other’s sensitive files or logs to external model providers, so leakage is plausible in default use.
conditions: IF both agents access the same directory, files read by one can be transmitted by the other.
IF RD-Agent logs contain secrets or sensitive datasets, Cursor can read them from the shared filesystem.
mitigations: Use separate directories and log paths.
Remove secrets from shared files before running either agent.
Restrict network egress for the shared workspace.
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor can execute shell commands, modify git state, and write the filesystem; RD-Agent also operates on files/logs and can call external APIs. In a shared repo, both can mutate the same working tree without coordination, making conflicting writes and git-state corruption likely.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same git checkout, concurrent edits can overwrite each other.
IF RD-Agent writes logs while Cursor rewrites files, state divergence can occur without locking.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Commit or stash changes before switching agents.
Use file locks for shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor’s agent loop can treat file content as actionable context, and RD-Agent produces research outputs, traces, and logs that may be consumed downstream. If Cursor acts on RD-Agent outputs without verification, a bad research result can cascade into code changes or commands with broad impact.
conditions: IF Cursor uses RD-Agent outputs as authoritative input, errors can propagate into edits or shell actions.
IF RD-Agent emits incorrect traces or logs, Cursor may incorporate them into subsequent steps without checking.
mitigations: Require human review before acting on RD-Agent outputs.
Cross-check key claims against source data.
Limit Cursor to read-only mode for RD-Agent artifacts.
Separate analysis and execution phases.
requires-engineering: add validation gates between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor handles source code, open files, and clipboard contents with broad egress, while RD-Agent handles financial reports, competition datasets, execution traces, logs, and multiple API keys. If regulated or proprietary data is placed in the shared workspace, the pair can create retention and residency mismatches; the profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace, both agents may retain or transmit it under different policies.
IF the operator relies on one agent’s deletion behavior, the other may still keep logs or buffers.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared folders.
Review retention settings for both tools.
Delete logs after each run.
Avoid placing secrets in prompts or files.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention policies.
